newsitem.title: USA: NYC revised Financial Plan still has gaps - McCall.
newsitem.headline: NYC revised Financial Plan still has gaps - McCall.

text.p: New York City's revised financial plan still has glaring gaps to the year 2000, and fails to address the continuing problem of structural balance, according to a report on the city's November Modification to its Financial Plan issued Thursday by State Comptroller H. Carl McCall.

"It's encouraging to see the City use a portion of $450 million in (fiscal year)1997 revenue to reduce some of the risks I and other fiscal monitors have indentified in the budget," McCall said in a release.

"But it's troubling to see continued large out-year gaps and reliance on one shots to balance the budget," he said. "The gap could be double what the City projects for FY 1998 and more than $4 billion by FY 2000.

McCall's report said the City has shifted certain risks in the Adopted Budget for FY 1997, such as the expectation of Port Authority payments and proceeds from the UN Plaza Hotel's sale, until future years. The modification also shows some reduction in out-year gaps mainly from a reduction in funding to the Health and Hospitals Corp (HHC).

"While the City needs to focus on HHC's financial future," McCall said, "this plan takes too optimistic a view of the changing market for health care and does not address the long-term impact of hospital privatization. More specifics are needed, particularly when changes in welfare and Medicaid will have such a profound effect on this organization."
The City still needs to confront the structural imbalance issue, and has yet to do so with its latest financial plan, the comptroller's report said.

"The City's expenditures grow by an annual rate of 5.5 percent compared with a revenue growth rate of just 1.1 percent over the next four years," McCall said. "It's easy to be seduced by the financial boom from good times on Wall Street, but that's an extremely volatile source of funds and the City can't build a solid financial future on an uncertain foundation."

As the City nears its debt limit, efforts to create new debt sources that are not part of a comprehensive debt management plan are "particularly disturbing," McCall said. His report again raised questions about the Infrastructure Finance Authority that would issue debt for education and transportation funding.

"This method of borrowing may circumvent the constitutional debt ceiling, but the Constitution is there for a reason," McCall said. "New Yorkers need to see a debt management plan that shows both the City can afford this rising debt burden and that the appropriate fiscal monitoring process is in place to ensure that debt is not allowed to grow unchecked."
While the city's numerous capital needs must be addressed, how those needs will be paid for must also be determined, he said.
"The City must construct a debt management plan to balance its pressing capital needs against its ability to pay," McCall said.

In citing the city's continued reliance on one-shot "gimmicks" to balance its budget, the report also pointed to items such as the sale of WNYC-TV, savings from City debt refunding, and anticipated receipt of state education aid for previous years as examples of non-recurring revenue streams that will dry up.

"Midway in the fiscal year there are encouraging signs that the City's budgetary risks for this year are diminished, but the long-term view remains uncertain and the financial risks and potential problems they pose for New Yorkers are very real," McCall said. "The City must try to resolve these issues for the City's ongoing fiscal health." --U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650
